issues.legal_issue: A proved custom treating a river’s deep stream as a constant village boundary can apply when the river changes course suddenly.
material_facts: Both sides accepted that the custom of dhar dhura existed, but disputed whether it covered sudden changes in the river’s course.
The recorded customary statement referred to land gained or lost through river action without specifying whether the action had to be gradual.
Prior official proceedings and a civil judgment recorded instances in which sudden changes were treated as changing the boundary under the custom.
The evidence showed that the custom had been established through local investigation and applied regardless of whether the river changed gradually or suddenly.
issues.conclusion: The evidence established that the custom applied to sudden changes in the river’s course, and the lower courts’ finding on this point was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2 of the Bengal Alluvion and Diluvion Regulation, 1825 recognises a clear and definite customary usage under which the main channel remains the boundary despite changes in the river’s course. The party asserting a custom that departs from general law bears the burden of proving it. As stated in Sibt Ali v. Muniruddin, evidence of a custom that transfers land whose character has not changed through river action must be scrutinised carefully, but cogent and satisfactory evidence can establish the custom.

predicates.customary_river_boundary_dispute: The proceeding concerns a claim to land whose boundary between estates is asserted to be determined by a customary river-channel rule.
predicates.custom_claimed_for_sudden_shifts: A party asserted that the customary boundary rule applied even when the river changed course suddenly.
predicates.cogent_evidence_establishes_sudden_shift: The party asserting the custom produced cogent evidence that the customary rule had been applied to sudden river-course changes.

issues.definition: When a customary river-boundary dispute involves a claim that the custom covers sudden shifts, and cogent evidence establishes that usage, the custom applies to sudden channel changes.

issues.legal_issue: The custom treating a river’s deep stream as a constant boundary is not unreasonable merely because river action can cause accidental gains or losses of land.
material_facts: The custom made gains and losses of land depend on changes in a river’s course, which can be accidental and uncertain.
The custom also provided a convenient way to settle boundaries and avoid disputes between neighbouring estates.
issues.conclusion: The custom was not unreasonable and was enforceable when established by the evidence.
issues.legal_principle: A custom must not be contrary to reason, but the relevant standard is legal reason rather than every person’s ordinary conception of reason. The Court referred to Coke on Littleton and noted that preventing quarrels and disputes between neighbouring estates is a community benefit; it also referred to the traditional deep-stream boundary rule discussed in Brihaspati and later commentators, and in Lal Mohan Doss’s work on riparian rights.

predicates.customary_river_boundary_dispute: The proceeding concerns a customary rule for determining boundaries between estates divided by a river.
predicates.custom_provides_a_convenient_boundary_ru: The custom provides a practical means of determining the boundary despite changes in the river’s course.
predicates.custom_prevents_neighbouring_estate_disp: The custom helps prevent boundary quarrels and disputes between neighbouring estate owners.

issues.definition: A customary river-boundary rule is not unreasonable when it supplies a convenient boundary method and helps prevent disputes between neighbouring estates.

issues.legal_issue: The deep-stream boundary custom ceases to govern the competing estates when the river moves entirely outside them and no longer divides them, leaving identifiable land to be determined under the governing alluvion and diluvion rules.
material_facts: The river suddenly left its former bed and flowed entirely outside the villages that it had divided.
The old bed remained identifiable, and the disputed land retained its character and identity.
Before the river moved outside the villages, the land had come under the claimant’s title while the river’s main stream divided the estates.
The river no longer divided the estates when the claim was determined.
issues.conclusion: The custom did not govern the land while the river flowed outside the estates; because the change was sudden and the land remained identifiable, the claimant was entitled to possess it under section 4, clause (2), of the Regulation. The High Court’s decision was reversed and the trial court’s judgment restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 2 of the Bengal Alluvion and Diluvion Regulation, 1825, the custom applies to determining boundaries between estates divided by the river. When the river ceases to divide those estates, the Regulation governs instead. Under section 4, clause (2), where a sudden river change leaves the character and identity of land intact, the original title may support a claim to that land.

rule.if: customary_river_boundary_dispute and river_flows_entirely_outside_the_estates and river_no_longer_divides_the_estates and land_remains_identifiable_after_sudden_change and claimant_held_title_before_the_shift

predicates.customary_river_boundary_dispute: The proceeding concerns a claim to land whose boundary was previously determined by a customary river-channel rule.
predicates.river_flows_entirely_outside_the_estates: The river’s main stream has moved so that it flows entirely outside the estates previously divided by it.
predicates.river_no_longer_divides_the_estates: The river no longer separates the estates whose boundary is in dispute.
predicates.land_remains_identifiable_after_sudden_c: The river changed course suddenly, and the disputed land retained its character and identity.
predicates.claimant_held_title_before_the_shift: The claimant held title to the land under the boundary rule before the river shifted outside the estates.

issues.definition: If the river suddenly moves outside estates it previously divided, the land remains identifiable, and the claimant held title before the move, the claimant’s original title governs the land.

issues.legal_issue: Rights under the deep-stream boundary custom revive when the river again flows within the estates it divides.
material_facts: The Court stated that the competing owners’ rights under the custom would revive if the river again came within the relevant village boundaries.
There was no evidence of the river’s position at the time of the appeal, so the decree was made subject to the custom being invoked if the proper occasion later arose.
issues.conclusion: The Court accepted that the rights under the custom would revive if the river again flowed within the villages, while making clear that the ruling was conditional on that future circumstance.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2 of the Bengal Alluvion and Diluvion Regulation, 1825 recognises a customary rule under which the deep stream is the constant boundary between estates divided by the river. The Court stated that the custom could again govern when the river returned within the villages it divides.

predicates.customary_river_boundary_dispute: The proceeding concerns rights to land claimed under a customary river-boundary rule.
predicates.established_deep_stream_custom: The parties have an established custom treating the river’s deep stream as the boundary between their estates.
predicates.river_again_flows_within_the_estates_it_: After flowing outside the estates, the river again flows within and divides those estates.

issues.definition: When an established deep-stream custom applies to a river boundary and the river again flows within the estates it divides, rights under that custom reactivate.
